title: AlphaFold: Protein Structure Prediction
hook: Predicting a protein's 3D shape from its sequence stumped biology for ~50 years. AlphaFold cracked it at near-experimental accuracy — and then released the structures to everyone.
key_points: Predicts a protein's folded 3D structure directly from its amino-acid sequence.
Reaches accuracy competitive with slow, costly experimental methods for many proteins.
Uses evolutionary information from related sequences plus attention-based deep learning.
Predicted structures for a vast swath of known proteins were released in a free public database.
content_html: John Jumper, Richard Evans, and the DeepMind team built AlphaFold to predict a protein's three-dimensional shape from just its amino-acid sequence — the long-standing "protein folding problem." The system reached accuracy rivaling experimental techniques for many proteins, a result widely seen as solving a roughly 50-year grand challenge in biology. They then released predicted structures for a huge fraction of known proteins in an open database, putting the results in the hands of researchers everywhere.
extra_html:
How it works

A protein is a chain of amino acids that folds into a specific shape, and that shape largely determines what the protein does. AlphaFold draws on evolutionary signal — patterns across many related sequences hint at which parts of the chain sit near each other — and feeds this into a deep network built on attention. It reasons jointly about the sequence and the emerging geometry, iteratively refining a 3D model of where every atom goes.

Why it matters

Knowing a protein's structure is central to understanding disease, designing drugs, and basic biology, but determining structures experimentally is slow and expensive. AlphaFold's accuracy meant many structures could be obtained in silico, and the open database of predictions accelerated work across the life sciences. It stands as a landmark example of deep learning delivering a genuine scientific breakthrough, not just a benchmark win.
